items.prompt: Where does most of the eye's focusing power come from?

options.label: The lens
options.feedback: The lens fine-tunes the focus, but it is not where most of the bending happens.

options.label: The cornea
options.feedback: Its fixed, curved surface bends incoming light more than any other part of the eye.

options.label: The pupil
options.feedback: The pupil only controls how much light gets in; it has no curve to bend light.

options.label: The retina
options.feedback: The retina is where the image lands and gets turned into signals — nothing there bends light on the way in.

items.ok_line: The biggest bend in the whole eye happens before the light gets anywhere near the lens.
items.ko_line: The part that does most of the work is fixed in shape, not the part that flexes.
items.exp_title: A fixed lens sat in front of the real one
items.exp_text: The cornea does most of the eye's focusing on its own, simply because it is the first curved surface a ray of light meets after leaving the air. Crossing from air into the denser, curved cornea bends the ray sharply, and that single bend aims it roughly toward the back of the eye before the lens ever gets involved.

items.prompt: How does the eye manage to focus on something close after looking at something far away?

options.label: The pupil widens
options.feedback: Pupil size controls how much light gets in, not how the eye focuses at different distances.

options.label: The eyeball changes length
options.feedback: The eyeball's shape stays fixed from one moment to the next; nothing inside it moves that fast.

options.label: Muscles reshape the lens
options.feedback: A ring of muscle around the lens squeezes or relaxes to change its curve.

options.label: The eye produces more tears
options.feedback: Tears keep the surface moist and clear; they play no part in bending light to a different point.

items.ok_line: One flexible part does the job that a camera needs a whole moving assembly for.
items.ko_line: Only one structure inside the eye is soft enough to change shape on command.
items.exp_title: A lens you can bulge on command
items.exp_text: Focusing on something near or far means bending light by a different amount, and the eye does that by changing the shape of its lens rather than moving anything else. A ring of muscle around the lens squeezes to let it bulge rounder for close objects, then relaxes to let it flatten again for anything far away.

items.prompt: Why does each eye have a small blind spot?

options.label: A patch of skin blocks the light there
options.feedback: No skin sits inside the eye; whatever blocks that spot is internal.

options.label: That patch never developed properly
options.feedback: It is not a flaw — every eye has one in the same place, by the way the wiring is laid out.

options.label: It is where old cells are being replaced
options.feedback: Cell replacement happens gradually across the whole retina, not massed at a single spot.

options.label: Nerve fibres bundle together and leave through that spot
options.feedback: Every signal-carrying fibre in the retina has to exit the eye at one shared point.

items.ok_line: Every wire in the retina has to leave through the same narrow gap.
items.ko_line: Something has to carry each cell's signal out of the eye, and it needs a way through.
items.exp_title: Where the wiring has to exit
items.exp_text: Every signal picked up around the retina has to leave the eye somehow, and all those nerve fibres gather into a single cable at one point before passing through the back wall. At that one gathering point there is no room left for any light-sensing cells, so whatever falls exactly there is never recorded at all.

items.prompt: Why does having two eyes help with judging how far away something is?

options.label: Each eye sees a slightly different view of the same scene
options.feedback: Comparing the two slightly different views is what gives a sense of depth.

options.label: Two eyes let you see twice as much detail
options.feedback: Sharpness comes from the receptors, not from having a spare eye; a single eye already sees full detail.

options.label: One eye rests while the other works
options.feedback: Both eyes are open and working together at once, not taking turns.

options.label: The second eye lets in extra light
options.feedback: More light would help in the dark, but darkness and distance are two different problems.

items.ok_line: Depth isn't seen directly — it's worked out from a mismatch.
items.ko_title: It isn't about brightness or sharpness
items.ko_line: Whatever the second eye contributes, it isn't more light and it isn't more detail.
items.exp_text: Because the eyes sit a short distance apart, each one looks at the world from a slightly different angle, and a nearby object shifts more between those two views than a distant one does. The visual system compares the two images and reads that shift as a measure of distance, turning the mismatch between the pictures into a sense of depth.

items.prompt: Why do both eyes turn together when you look to one side?

options.label: Only one eye actually moves and the other follows the image
options.feedback: Both eyeballs physically rotate at the same time; neither one is a passive follower.

options.label: The eyes are physically joined behind the nose
options.feedback: The two eyeballs sit in separate sockets with no physical connection between them.

options.label: Muscles around each eye are driven together
options.feedback: Matching muscles in each socket are wired to fire together rather than independently.

options.label: Turning the head pulls both eyes along automatically
options.feedback: Eyes turn together even when the head stays perfectly still, so head movement cannot be the reason.

items.ok_line: Two separate eyeballs, moved by a single coordinated command.
items.ko_title: Not the head, and not one eye alone
items.ko_line: Cover the head's movement and the eyes still turn together — so look at what drives the eyes themselves.
items.exp_title: Six muscles per eye, matched in pairs
items.exp_text: Each eyeball sits in a sling of six small muscles that pull it up, down, left, right and in between, and the matching muscles in the two sockets are driven to fire together rather than independently. Pull the muscle that swings the left eye rightward and the matching muscle in the right eye tightens at the same moment, so the two eyeballs swivel as a single unit.

items.prompt: What does the picture that lands on the back of the eye actually look like?

options.label: Upside down and reversed left to right
options.feedback: Bending light the way the eye does turns the picture over both ways.

options.label: The right way up, just smaller
options.feedback: Bending light the way the eye does turns the image over; nothing keeps it upright before it reaches the back wall.

options.label: Blurred until it reaches the brain
options.feedback: Sharpness depends on focus, which is settled before the image lands; that's a separate matter from which way up it is.

options.label: Split into two halves
options.feedback: Light rays converge into a single unbroken image; nothing physical divides it in two.

items.ok_line: The picture never arrives right-side up in the first place.
items.ko_title: Think about what bending light does
items.ko_line: Rays that start high end up low, and rays that start on one side end up on the other.
items.exp_title: A picture flipped by its own focusing
items.exp_text: When curved surfaces bend light toward a point, rays that start high end up crossing to arrive low, and rays that start on one side cross over to the other — the same crossing any simple lens produces. The cornea and lens both bend light that way, so the picture forming at the back of the eye lands flipped from the scene it came from, top to bottom and side to side.

items.prompt: Why do you blink even when nothing is bothering your eyes?

options.label: To rest the eye muscles
options.feedback: The muscles doing the blinking are different from the ones that focus or move the eye, so blinking gives those no rest at all.

options.label: To let more light in periodically
options.feedback: Closing the eye blocks light rather than letting more in.

options.label: To signal to others
options.feedback: Blinking happens just as often alone in the dark as in company, so it cannot be there for anyone else to see.

options.label: To spread a film of tears across the surface
options.feedback: Each blink draws a fresh layer of tear fluid across the eye.

items.ok_line: Blinking is maintenance, running quietly in the background all day.
items.ko_title: Not for rest, light, or company
items.ko_line: Blinking happens exactly as often when you're completely alone, in a lit room, doing nothing tiring.
items.exp_title: A wipe that keeps the front of the eye wet
items.exp_text: The eyelid works like a wiper blade, drawing a thin layer of tear fluid across the cornea every time it closes and reopens. That constant, quiet re-coating keeps the surface smooth and clear and washes away whatever dust has settled on it since the last blink.

items.prompt: Why does the cornea have no blood vessels running through it, unlike almost every other living tissue?

options.label: It doesn't need any oxygen to survive
options.feedback: Corneal cells are alive and do need oxygen; they simply get it another way.

options.label: It is not made of living cells
options.feedback: The cornea is built of living, working cells — which is exactly why it needs a way to get oxygen without vessels running through it.

options.label: Blood vessels would block the light passing through
options.feedback: Blood and vessel walls are not transparent, so any vessel there would cast a shadow.

options.label: It grows too fast for vessels to keep up
options.feedback: The cornea is one of the more stable tissues in the body, not one growing quickly.

items.ok_line: The one tissue in the body that light has to pass straight through stays free of the vessels almost everything else needs.
items.ko_title: Think about what light can pass through
items.ko_line: The cornea is alive and needs oxygen just like other tissue — so why would it be built without the usual way of getting it?
items.exp_title: Clear only by staying empty of vessels
items.exp_text: Any blood vessel running through the cornea would cast a shadow and scatter light on its way to the back of the eye, since blood and vessel walls are not transparent. So the cornea gets its oxygen a different way, drawing it directly from the tear film and the air rather than from blood, and stays perfectly clear as a result.

items.prompt: What keeps the front chamber of the eye rounded and firm rather than collapsing inward?

options.label: The bones of the eye socket press it into shape
options.feedback: The socket surrounds the eye but never touches its front surface.

options.label: A clear fluid inside is constantly produced and drained
options.feedback: A steady flow of fluid keeps the chamber under a small, constant pressure.

options.label: The eyelid holds the shape closed
options.feedback: The eye keeps its rounded shape even wide open, so the eyelid cannot be what is holding it.

options.label: The lens expands to fill the space
options.feedback: The lens sits behind this chamber and stays roughly the same size; it does not swell to fill anything.

items.ok_line: A shape held up by flow, the way a hose stays firm only while water runs through it.
items.ko_line: Take away the eyelid, the socket, even the lens, and the front of the eye would still hold its shape — so look for what's actually pushing outward.
items.exp_title: A fluid that is always flowing and always full
items.exp_text: Tissue behind the cornea continuously makes a clear, watery fluid, and other tissue nearby continuously drains it away at close to a matching rate. That steady flow keeps the chamber full under a small, constant pressure, and it is that pressure, pushing outward evenly in every direction, that holds the cornea in its rounded shape.

items.prompt: Why does even a tiny speck of dust on the cornea make you blink immediately, before you can even decide to?

options.label: The cornea is packed with nerve endings
options.feedback: Even the lightest touch there is picked up strongly and routed into a reflex.

options.label: Dust is heavier than it looks
options.feedback: Weight has nothing to do with it; a speck too light to feel on skin still triggers an instant blink on the cornea.

options.label: The eye has no defences against dust
options.feedback: The blink itself is the defence, and it works within a fraction of a second.

options.label: The cornea swells around any object that touches it
options.feedback: Swelling, if it happens at all, takes far longer than the blink that follows contact almost instantly.

items.ok_title: Wired to react first, think later
items.ok_line: The eyelid closes before there's even time to notice what landed there.
items.ko_title: It isn't weight, and it isn't a weakness
items.ko_line: A speck too light to feel anywhere else on the body still sets off an instant blink here — ask what's different about this surface.
items.exp_title: A surface wired to react before you think
items.exp_text: The cornea carries a dense web of nerve endings, packed far more thickly there than in most of the skin, so even the lightest touch is picked up strongly. That signal travels a short, direct route into a reflex that closes the eyelid automatically, acting before there is time for any conscious decision.
